unit.title: Follow principles of Occupational Health and Safety (OH&S) in work environment

summary: This unit teaches you to apply the principles of occupational health and safety (OH&S) as a team leader in welding and fabrication. You will learn to assess risks with a risk matrix and control them in the right order; deal with fume, noise, heat, electricity, hot work, gas cylinders, confined spaces, work at height and heavy lifts; respond to emergencies and give first aid; and report, investigate and inspect so that the same accident does not happen twice.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). At Level 2 you learned to work safely yourself. At Level 3 you are responsible for **other people's safety too**: you assess the risks of a job before it starts, choose and set up the controls, issue or work under permits, supervise trainees, respond to incidents, investigate what went wrong, and check that the workplace stays safe.

Welding and fabrication combine many serious hazards: electricity, intense light, toxic fume, fire, compressed gases, heavy steel, sharp edges, noise, heat, and work in tanks and at height. Most injuries are not bad luck. They follow from hazards that were known, controls that were skipped, and warnings that were not passed on.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders and fabricators who lead a team or a site job.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Know your duties and rights
Understand what the law and your employer expect of you, of your team and of management; stop unsafe work; build a good safety culture.
Assess risks
Break a job into steps, find the hazards, score the risks with a matrix, and record it in a job safety analysis (JSA).
Control risks in the right order
Eliminate, substitute, engineer, organise, then protect with PPE; check what risk is left.
Control welding health hazards
Fume, gases, radiation, noise, heat and chemicals: extraction, respirators, safety data sheets and welfare.
Work safely with electricity, machines, fire and gases
Electrical safety in damp places, lockout and tagout, hot work permits, fire watch, extinguishers, gas cylinders and flashback.
Plan high-risk work
Confined spaces, work at height, manual handling and crane lifts.
Respond to emergencies
Raise the alarm, evacuate, and give first aid for burns, eye injuries, shock, cuts and heat illness.
Report, investigate and inspect
Report incidents and near misses, find root causes, write the report, carry out inspections and follow actions through to the end.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on risk assessment, the order of controls, fume, confined spaces, hot work, gas cylinders, electricity, isolation, noise, PPE, lifting, height, fire, emergencies, first aid, investigation and safety culture.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as residual risk, LEV, phosgene, flashback arrestor, root cause and heatstroke) and essays on planning and controlling high-risk work.

Two **group practicals**: a job safety analysis, hot work permit and site set-up for a welding job outside the shop; and investigating a staged incident, giving first aid and writing the incident report.

blocks.note: Learn the order of controls by heart (eliminate, substitute, engineer, administrate, PPE) and be able to give a welding example of each. Many questions test whether you can pick the control that sits highest in that order.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Jamaica's **Factories Act** and its regulations have long set safety duties for workshops and factories, and the **Ministry of Labour and Social Security**, through its Occupational Safety and Health Department, inspects workplaces and investigates serious accidents. A broader occupational safety and health law has been in preparation for some years. Your instructor will tell you which laws are in force now; the principles below apply whatever the law's exact wording.

head: Who
Main duties
rows: Employer and managers
Provide a safe workplace, safe equipment and safe systems of work
Assess risks and put controls in place
Give information, training and supervision
Provide PPE free of charge, and first aid and welfare facilities
Consult workers on safety
Report serious accidents to the authorities as the law requires
Supervisors and team leaders
Plan work safely and brief the team
Make sure controls, permits and PPE are used
Stop unsafe work and correct unsafe acts
Coach trainees and watch them until they are competent
Report hazards, incidents and near misses, and follow up actions
Every worker and trainee
Follow safe procedures and use the PPE provided
Take care of your own safety and that of others
Report hazards, damage, incidents and near misses
Never misuse or interfere with safety equipment
Not work under the influence of alcohol or drugs
Contractors and visitors
Follow the site's rules, inductions and permits
Report to the person in charge before starting

ul: **The right to know:** to be told about the hazards of the work and trained to work safely.
**The right to take part:** to be consulted about safety, for example through a safety committee or safety representative.

**The right to refuse:** to stop or refuse work they honestly believe is dangerous, such as cutting open a drum that held fuel and has not been made safe, without being punished. A good supervisor backs that refusal and has the danger removed first.

blocks.p: **Safety culture** is how people really behave about safety, especially when no one is watching. In a good safety culture:

ul: leaders set the example: they wear their PPE and follow the rules every time;
people report hazards and near misses freely, and see them acted on quickly;
the aim of an investigation is to find causes, not to blame, so people tell the truth;
workers are asked for ideas, and any worker can stop a job that looks unsafe;
unsafe acts are stopped calmly and corrected at once; good practice is praised.

blocks.p: If you see someone working unsafely, **stop them**, explain the danger, show the safe way, and check they follow it. For example, a trainee who lifts his helmet to see the joint just as he strikes is exposing his eyes to the arc: stop him and coach him to set up the electrode and his body position first, then lower the helmet before striking.

Anyone who comes onto the site, such as a contractor repairing the overhead crane, signs in, receives a site induction (hazards, emergency routes, PPE, rules), works under the right permits and lockouts, and is escorted where needed. Visitors and clients are kept away from arc light, sparks and lifts.

A **hazard** is anything that can cause harm: electricity, fume, a heavy plate, a hot surface. A **risk** is how likely the harm is to happen **and** how bad it would be. A hazard you never come near has low risk; the same hazard met every day without controls has high risk.

head: Kind of hazard
Examples in welding and fabrication
rows: Physical
Arc light and UV, noise, heat, vibration, electricity, moving machinery
Chemical
Welding fume and gases, solvents, paints, pickling paste, acids
Fire and explosion
Sparks and spatter, fuel gases, oxygen, containers that held fuel
Mechanical and handling
Heavy or sharp steel, crush points, falling loads, grinders
Environment
Work at height, confined spaces, wet ground, Jamaica's sun and heat, traffic on site
People and organisation
Fatigue, rushing, poor training, poor communication, lone working

flow: Break the job into its steps (unload, set out, cut, fit, weld, grind, paint, fit on site)
For each step, list the hazards, including hidden ones such as the far side of a wall
Score each risk with the risk matrix
Choose controls, working down the order of controls
Score the risk again with the controls in place: this is the residual risk
Record it, brief the team, and have everyone sign it
Review it if anything changes: a new site, new people, the weather, an incident

blocks.p: Many workplaces score **likelihood** and **severity** from 1 to 5 each, and multiply them: **risk score = likelihood × severity**.

head: Score
Likelihood
Severity
rows: Rare: hardly ever
Insignificant: no injury
Unlikely
Minor: first aid only
Possible
Moderate: medical treatment or time off work
Likely
Major: serious injury, hospital stay
Almost certain
Catastrophic: death or permanent disability

head: Risk score
Rating (a typical banding)
What to do
rows: 1 to 4
Low
Carry on with normal care; keep under review
5 to 10
Medium
Reduce the risk further where you reasonably can; supervise
High
Do not start until more controls bring it down
Very high
Stop: the job must not go ahead as planned

blocks.p: **Worked example:** burns to a passer-by from arc flash while fitting a gate on a busy pavement: likely (4) × moderate (3) = **12, high**. With screens round the work and the area taped off, it becomes unlikely (2) × moderate (3) = **6, medium**: acceptable with supervision. The 6 is the **residual risk**, the risk left after the controls are in place.

blocks.note: The bands above are typical; your workplace's matrix may use different words or cut-off points. Use the one your company or Centre has adopted, and use it the same way every time.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Controls are chosen from the top of this list down. The higher the control, the less it depends on people doing the right thing every time. PPE is the **last line of defence**, not the first.

head: Level
What it means
Welding and fabrication examples
rows: 1. Eliminate
Remove the hazard completely
Weld the frame on the ground, then lift it into place (no work at height); bolt panels instead of welding them on site (no hot work there)
2. Substitute
Replace it with something less hazardous
A water-based degreaser instead of a chlorinated solvent; a lower-fume process; ungalvanised steel welded first and galvanised after
3. Engineering controls
Physical measures that isolate people from the hazard
Fume extraction at the weld, welding screens, machine guards, a voltage-reducing device, flashback arrestors, guardrails
4. Administrative controls
Rules, systems and training that change how people work
Hot work and confined space permits, a fire watch, lockout and tagout, safe work procedures, training, signs, limiting time in noise or heat
5. Personal protective equipment (PPE)
Equipment worn by the person
Helmet, gloves, flame-resistant clothing, safety boots, ear protection, respirator

blocks.p: Most jobs need a mix: for example, extraction (engineering) plus a fire watch (administrative) plus a respirator (PPE). If the risk is still high after the controls you have chosen, add more controls before any work starts.

ul: Clear hot slag, offcuts and electrode stubs during the shift, not only at the end: they cause trips, burns and fires.
Keep walkways, exits and fire equipment clear; run welding leads and hoses where people will not trip on them.
Mark hot metal HOT; store steel in racks, not leaning against walls.
Put up the right safety signs, and take down warnings that no longer apply.

sections.title: Fume, gases, noise, heat and chemicals

blocks.p: Welding fume is a cloud of very fine metal particles, small enough to go deep into the lungs, mixed with gases. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classes welding fume, including mild steel fume, as a cause of cancer in people. Short-term effects include irritation, coughing and metal fume fever; long-term effects include lung disease and cancer.

head: Metal or coating
What the fume holds
Main harm
Extra controls
rows: Mild steel
Iron oxide, manganese
Lung disease and cancer over years; manganese can damage the nervous system
Extraction at the weld; respirator if extraction is not enough
Galvanised (zinc-coated) steel
Zinc oxide
**Metal fume fever**: chills, fever, aches, metallic taste, a few hours after welding
Remove the zinc from the weld area where the procedure allows; extraction; respirator
Stainless steel
Chromium (including hexavalent chromium) and nickel compounds
Lung cancer, asthma, skin and nose damage
Extraction at the source is essential; a suitable respirator is often needed too
Painted or primed steel
Breakdown products of the paint; lead from old paint
Irritation; lead poisoning
Strip the paint well back from the weld; check old paint for lead
Cadmium-plated bolts and parts (they can look like ordinary zinc plating, so check before welding)
Cadmium oxide
Very toxic: can damage the lungs and kidneys, and can kill
Do not weld until the plating is removed and specialist controls are in place

ul: **Ozone** forms when the arc's UV light acts on the air, especially with MIG and TIG on stainless steel and aluminium. It irritates the eyes, nose and lungs.
**Carbon monoxide** comes from carbon dioxide shielding gas breaking down in the arc, and from engine exhausts. It is invisible and has no smell.
**Shielding gases** such as argon and carbon dioxide are heavier than air. In a tank, pit or low space they collect and push out the oxygen, and a person can collapse without warning.

**Phosgene**, a very toxic gas, can form when the arc's UV light acts on the vapour of **chlorinated solvent** degreasers. Keep such solvents well away from welding, and let parts dry fully before welding them; better, use a non-chlorinated degreaser.

**Local exhaust ventilation (LEV)**, such as an extraction arm or on-torch extraction, captures fume at the source before it reaches the welder. Its pull falls off very quickly with distance, so keep the hood close to the arc and move it as you move along the weld.
Check that the extraction works before you start (feel the airflow, or watch the fume being drawn in), and report it at once if it does not.
**Keep your head out of the plume** that rises from the weld: it carries the fume straight to your nose and mouth.
General ventilation (open doors, fans) helps, but it is not enough on its own for regular welding indoors.
Clean coatings, oil and paint from the weld area first; read the SDS for each filler and product.
Use RPE when extraction alone does not keep the fume down, and as the risk assessment says. A disposable or half-mask respirator must be **rated for welding fume** (fine particles).
A tight-fitting respirator works only if it **seals** to the face. Each wearer should be **fit tested** for the model they use, and do a quick **fit check** every time they put it on.
Stubble or a beard where the mask seals lets fume leak in around the edges. A worker with a beard needs a loose-fitting powered respirator, such as a welding helmet with filtered air blown in.
Keep RPE clean and stored in a bag or box; change filters as the maker says; throw away damaged disposable masks.
A supervisor checks that each worker's respirator fits, is the right type and is worn correctly.

blocks.h: Hazardous substances and safety data sheets

blocks.p: Every chemical product (primers, paints, thinners, degreasers, anti-spatter sprays, pickling paste) must come with a **safety data sheet (SDS)** from the supplier. Read it **before** the product is used. If a product arrives without one, get the SDS from the supplier first, and do not use the product until you have it.

ul: The SDS tells you the hazards, the safe handling and storage, the PPE and ventilation needed, first aid, fire-fighting, spills and disposal.

Container labels carry warning pictograms (red diamonds): for example a flame (flammable), a skull (toxic), corrosion (burns skin and eyes), and a figure with a damaged chest (long-term health hazard).

Stainless steel pickling paste usually contains strong acids, often including hydrofluoric acid, whose burns may not hurt at first but go deep. Its SDS names special first aid; have it, and an eyewash, ready before the paste is opened.

blocks.p: Grinding, hammering, gouging and cutting are loud enough to damage hearing. **Noise-induced hearing loss** builds up slowly, without pain, and **cannot be cured**. It often comes with tinnitus, a constant ringing in the ears.

ul: A rough guide: if you have to raise your voice to talk to someone about 2 m away, the noise should be measured; if you have to shout to be heard at about 1 m, it is almost certainly at a harmful level.
An angle grinder is typically around 95 to 105 dB(A). On the rule most safety bodies use, every **3 dB** more is twice the sound energy, so the safe exposure time is halved.
Inside a steel tank or container, sound bounces off the walls and builds up, so the same tool is louder there.

Controls: quieter tools and methods, damping and enclosures, distance, less time in noise, then hearing protection worn **all the time** in the noise. Plugs and muffs must fit; wearing them for only part of the time gives much less protection than people think.

blocks.p: Jamaica's heat, the radiant heat of the arc and the preheated steel, and heavy flame-resistant clothing together put welders at real risk of heat illness, especially inside tanks, containers and roof spaces, and on sunny afternoons.

ul: Drink water often (as a guide, a cup every 15 to 20 minutes during hard work in the heat), before you feel thirsty.
Plan hot, heavy work for the cooler hours; give shade and rest breaks in a cool place; use fans and forced ventilation in enclosed spaces.
New workers, and workers back from leave, need a few days to get used to the heat: give them lighter work at first.
Never let welders roll up sleeves or work in vests to keep cool: arc rays burn bare skin in minutes.
Watch each other for the signs of heat exhaustion and heatstroke (see the first aid section).

blocks.p: A safe workplace also provides drinking water, toilets, washing facilities with soap, a clean place to eat away from the work area, and first aid. Wash your hands and face before eating, drinking or smoking, so you do not swallow metal dust.

The danger in welding comes mainly from the machine's **open-circuit voltage**, which is present at the electrode, the holder and the torch whenever the machine is on, even when you are not welding. A shock is far more likely when the welder's body is wet with sweat, the gloves are damp, or the welder is lying, kneeling or sitting on steel. In Jamaica's heat these conditions are common.

ul: Inspect the machine, the input lead, the welding leads, the holder and the work clamp before use: no cuts, bare copper, cracked insulation or loose connections.
Wear dry leather gloves and dry clothing; change gloves when they get wet; never change an electrode with bare or wet hands.
Stand or kneel on a dry insulating mat or board on wet ground or steel floors.

Fix the **work clamp** to clean metal on the job, as close to the weld as possible. If it is far away, welding current can stray through other paths: lifting chains, machine bearings, building steel or the earth wires of other equipment, which it can overheat and burn out.

In damp, hot or cramped places, such as inside a tank, use a machine fitted with a **voltage-reducing device (VRD)**, which lowers the open-circuit voltage when you are not welding, or a DC machine made for such places, as the procedure says.
Machines must be correctly earthed on their supply side and fed from a properly protected supply. Only a qualified electrician works on mains wiring, plugs and sockets.

blocks.p: If a welding machine's input lead is cut through its outer sheath, or any electrical equipment is damaged, the supervisor **isolates it, tags it 'Do not use'**, takes it out of service, and has it repaired by a competent person. Tape is not a repair. Portable tools should carry a current inspection tag.

ul: Keep guards on grinders, guillotines, saws, presses and drills. A missing guard is a reason to stop the machine.
Check that the grinding disc is the right type and is rated for at least the grinder's speed, and is not cracked or damaged.
Never reach into a machine to clear a jam, adjust it or clean it while it can move: isolate it first.

blocks.p: **Lockout and tagout** stops a machine being started while someone is working on it. A tag on its own is only a warning; a **lock** on the isolator is what stops it.

flow: Plan: identify every energy source (electrical, hydraulic, air, springs, raised parts that can fall)
Tell the people affected that the machine is being shut down
Shut the machine down normally
Isolate each energy source at its isolator
Fit **your own** padlock and a tag with your name, the date and the reason
Release or block stored energy: bleed air or hydraulic pressure, block raised parts
**Try it:** check that the machine cannot start (press start with the isolator locked off, or test as the procedure says), then return the controls to off
Do the work
When finished: remove tools, refit guards, warn people, then remove **your own** lock and tag only

ul: When several people work on the same machine, each fits his or her own lock to a **multi-lock hasp**, so the machine cannot be started until the last person has finished and removed their lock.
Never remove someone else's lock or tag. If a lock is left on and its owner has gone home, the supervisor follows the workplace's special procedure to find the person and check that it is safe.
Removing a tag or lock to 'just finish a cut' is a serious breach and must be treated as a near miss.

sections.title: Hot work, fire and gas cylinders

blocks.p: **Hot work** is welding, cutting, grinding, brazing or anything else that makes sparks or heat that could start a fire. Outside the welding shop it needs a **hot work permit** from the person in charge of the area.

flow: The area is inspected by a competent person before work starts
Anything that can burn is moved well away (often about 10 m or more), or covered with fire-resisting blankets
Gaps in floors, walls and ceilings are covered, so sparks cannot fall or blow through
The **far side** of walls, partitions, floors and pipes is checked: heat travels through steel and can set fire to things out of sight
Drums, tanks and pipes that held fuel or chemicals are not touched until a competent person has made them safe
A suitable extinguisher and a fire blanket are placed at hand; screens protect other people from arc light
The permit records the job, the place, the times, the precautions, and the names of the welder and the fire watch
A trained **fire watch** stays during the work and for the time the permit sets afterwards (often 30 to 60 minutes), checking for smoke and smouldering
The area is checked again, and the permit is signed off and returned

blocks.note: Never weld or cut a drum, tank or pipe that has held fuel, oil or chemicals until a competent person has cleaned it, tested it and declared it safe. A few drops of fuel left inside are enough to make vapour that explodes when heated.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A fire needs **heat**, **fuel** and **oxygen** (the fire triangle). Take away any one and the fire goes out: cooling removes heat, smothering removes oxygen, and clearing combustibles removes fuel.

head: Extinguisher
Use it on
Never use it on
Notes
rows: Water
Wood, paper, cloth, rubbish
Burning oil or fuel; live electrical equipment
Cools the burning material
Foam
Wood, paper, cloth; flammable liquids
Live electrical equipment (unless the label says it is tested for it)
Smothers a liquid fire and cools
Carbon dioxide (CO2)
Live electrical equipment; small flammable-liquid fires
Deep-seated fires in wood or paper; it does not cool much
The horn gets very cold: hold the handle; less effective outdoors in wind
Dry powder (ABC)
Most fires: solids, liquids, electrical
Cooking oil and fat fires
Messy; the cloud of powder makes it hard to see
Wet chemical
Cooking oil and fat fires
Electrical fires
For kitchens

blocks.p: Read the label: it shows in words and pictures which fires the extinguisher is for. Many extinguishers in Jamaica carry American class letters (A ordinary solids, B flammable liquids, C live electrical equipment, D metals, K cooking oils); European ones use C for gases and F for cooking oils.

ul: Raise the alarm first. Fight a fire only if it is small, you are trained, and your way out is behind you.
Remember **PASS**: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, Sweep from side to side.
Report every use of an extinguisher, even a short one, so it is recharged or replaced.
Store cylinders **upright and secured** with a chain or strap, in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place, out of direct sun and away from heat, sparks, oil and grease.
Keep **oxygen apart from fuel gases** such as acetylene and propane, by the distance your rules give (often about 6 m) or by a fire-resisting wall. If a fire starts, oxygen makes it far fiercer.
Keep full and empty cylinders apart and labelled; keep valve caps or guards on cylinders not in use.
Move cylinders on a proper trolley, secured; never drag them, drop them, roll them on their sides or lift them by the valve.
Transport them upright and secured, with valves closed and regulators removed, in a ventilated vehicle, never in a closed car boot.

Inside an acetylene cylinder, the acetylene is dissolved in **acetone** held in a porous filling. That is why acetylene cylinders must be used **upright**: on its side, acetone can be drawn out into the hoses and regulator. If one has been lying down, stand it upright and wait the time the supplier gives before use.
Fit the right regulators, with **flashback arrestors** at the regulators (and non-return valves at the torch, as the maker says).
Check every connection for leaks with **leak-test solution** brushed on: bubbles show a leak. Never use a flame to look for leaks.
Keep oil and grease away from oxygen fittings: oil in pure oxygen can burst into flame.
Never use oxygen to blow dust off clothes, to cool yourself, or to 'freshen' the air: clothing soaked in oxygen burns fiercely.
Acetylene becomes unstable at high pressure: never set its regulator above the maximum the supplier gives.
Close the cylinder valves when work stops, and take hoses and torches out of tanks and enclosed spaces at breaks.

head: Event
What happens
What to do
rows: Gas leak (for example a smell of acetylene)
Gas escapes from a cylinder, regulator or hose
Put out flames and stop hot work nearby; close the cylinder valve if it is safe; ventilate; keep people away; if it cannot be stopped, evacuate and call the supplier or the fire service
Backfire
A loud pop at the nozzle; the flame may go out or relight
Close the torch valves; find the cause (nozzle too close to the work, overheated or dirty nozzle, wrong pressures) before relighting
Flashback
The flame burns back inside the torch or hose, often with a hiss or squeal and a hot handle
Close the torch valves at once (most makers say the oxygen valve first), then the cylinder valves; let it cool; do not use it again until the cause is found and the equipment checked
Cylinder heated in a fire
A heated acetylene cylinder can explode, even some time later
Evacuate the area, call the fire service (dial 110), and tell them it is an acetylene cylinder; do not go near it

sections.title: Confined spaces, height, manual handling and lifting

blocks.p: A **confined space** is an enclosed or partly enclosed space with limited ways in and out, where bad air can build up: tanks, vessels, silos, pits, sewers, large pipes and ducts, boat hulls. People die in them from lack of oxygen, toxic or flammable gas, fire, heat and drowning, and **many of those who die are untrained rescuers** who went in to help.

flow: First ask: can the work be done from outside, so that nobody needs to go in?
If entry is needed, plan it and issue a **confined space entry permit**
Isolate the space: blank or disconnect pipes, lock off pumps, mixers and power
Clean it if needed, and find out what it held and what it was cleaned with
A trained person tests the air with a gas detector for oxygen, flammable gas and toxic gas, at the top, middle and bottom, before entry and during the work
Ventilate with fresh air blown in by a fan; **never use oxygen** to freshen the air
Keep gas cylinders outside; take hoses and torches out at every break
Use dry PPE, an insulating mat, a VRD or suitable DC machine, and low-voltage or battery lighting
A trained **standby person** stays at the entry the whole time, keeps in contact, never goes in, and has a rescue plan and equipment ready
Close the permit when everyone is out

ul: Normal air has about **20.9% oxygen**. Most entry permits allow entry only when the oxygen reading is between about **19.5% and 23.5%**. Below that, people become confused and collapse; above it, clothing, hair and grease catch fire easily and burn fiercely.
Gases that are heavier than air, such as argon, carbon dioxide and propane, sink to the bottom of a tank or pit; others rise. That is why the air is tested at several levels.
If the alarm sounds or anyone feels unwell, everyone gets out at once.

blocks.p: Falls from height are among the commonest causes of serious injury in fabrication and construction. Follow the order: **avoid** working at height where you can, **prevent** falls where you cannot, and **arrest** a fall only as the last choice.

ul: **Avoid:** fabricate and weld on the ground, then lift the finished frame into place.

**Prevent:** work from a scaffold or platform with guardrails and toe boards, or a mobile elevating work platform (MEWP) used by a trained operator. Scaffolds are put up and inspected by competent people.

**Arrest:** a harness and lanyard fixed to a strong anchor, with a rescue plan. For hot work, use lanyards made to resist sparks and spatter (for example with a steel wire core); ordinary webbing can melt or burn through.

Ladders are for short, light jobs and for getting up and down. Set them at about 1 in 4 (75°), tie or foot them, extend them about 1 m above the landing, and keep three points of contact. **Do not weld from a ladder**: a shock, a flash or a burn can make you let go and fall.
Keep people out from under work at height; stop tools and offcuts falling.

blocks.p: Steel is heavy. Mild steel weighs about **7,850 kg per cubic metre**, so 1 mm of thickness weighs about **7.85 kg per square metre**. Work out the weight before you lift.

**Worked example:** a plate 2.0 m × 1.0 m × 8 mm: 2.0 m² × 8 × 7.85 kg = **about 126 kg**. That is far too heavy for one person, and too heavy to carry safely by hand even for a team: use a plate trolley, a crane or a forklift.

ul: Plan the lift: the weight, the route, where it will be set down, and who will help.
Use lifting aids wherever you can: trolleys, pallet trucks, cranes, chain blocks, plate clamps.
For a lift by hand: a firm stance, bend the knees, keep the load close to the body, do not twist, lift smoothly. For a team lift, one person gives the commands.
Wear gloves for sharp edges and safety boots for dropped steel.
Every crane, chain block, sling, shackle and plate clamp is marked with its **safe working load (SWL)**, also called the working load limit (WLL), and has a current inspection record or tag.

Before use, check the tag and look for damage: stretched or cracked chain links, opened or bent hooks, missing safety catches, cut or burnt webbing slings, broken wires or kinks in wire rope. Damaged gear is tagged out of use.

The SWL must be more than the load plus the slings and clamps. The wider the angle between sling legs, the more force in each leg: at 120° between the legs, each leg carries the full weight of the load. Keep the angle at 90° or less.

Use the right attachment: plate clamps for plate (vertical clamps for lifting single plates on edge; horizontal clamps in pairs on a spreader or two-leg sling for flat plates), never a single sling that the plate can slide out of.
One trained person gives the signals. Lift a little first and check the balance; use tag lines to control swing; land the load on timber bearers.
**Never stand or walk under a suspended load**, and never ride on one.
Every workplace needs a written emergency plan: how the alarm is raised, the escape routes, the assembly point, who calls the emergency services, and who checks each area.
**Wardens** check their area during an evacuation so that every room, toilet and store is checked and nobody is left behind. A roll call at the assembly point confirms everyone is out.
Keep exits and escape routes clear and unlocked during working hours; practise with drills.

Post the emergency numbers by the phone: in Jamaica, **110** for fire and ambulance and **119** for police. Give the address and a clear landmark, since many Jamaican addresses are hard for an ambulance to find, and send someone to meet it.
Never go back into a building until the person in charge says it is safe.

blocks.note: The hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November. Before a storm, secure or bring in loose roof sheets, steel stock and cylinders, which can become missiles in high winds; shut down and protect equipment; and check the site for damage, fallen lines and flooding before work restarts.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Know who the trained first aiders are and where the first aid kit, the eyewash and the emergency phone are. In any emergency: check for **danger** to yourself first, then the casualty's **response**, call for **help**, and check **airway** and **breathing**. Wear disposable gloves when dealing with blood.

head: Injury
First aid
Do not
rows: Burn from hot metal, spatter or flame
Cool the burn under cool running water for about 20 minutes
Remove rings and watches near it before it swells
Cover loosely with cling film or a clean, non-fluffy dressing
Get medical help for large, deep or electrical burns, or burns to the face, hands or groin
Use ice, butter, creams or toothpaste; burst blisters; pull off clothing or metal stuck to the burn
Chemical splash in the eye (such as pickling acid)
Rinse it at once at the eyewash or with clean running water, holding the eyelid open, for **at least 15 minutes**
Then get medical help, taking the SDS with you
Rub the eye, or wait to see if it gets better
Grinding particle in the eye
Rinse gently with eyewash
If it is stuck in the eye, cover the eye and get medical help
Try to dig out a particle that is stuck
Arc eye (flash burn)
Rest in a dim place; a cool, damp cloth over closed eyes may ease it
See a doctor or nurse
Rub the eyes
Electric shock
Switch off or isolate before you touch the person
If you cannot, push them clear with something dry that does not conduct
Call 110; check breathing; give CPR if trained and needed
Anyone who has had a shock sees a doctor
Touch the person while they may still be live
Bleeding cut
Press firmly on the wound with a clean dressing
Raise the injured part if you can
Get medical help for deep cuts
Remove an object stuck deep in a wound

head: Point
Heat exhaustion
Heatstroke
rows: Signs
Heavy sweating; pale, cool and clammy skin; headache; dizziness; feeling sick; cramps; tiredness; fast pulse. The person is still thinking clearly
Very high body temperature; hot skin, which may be dry or still sweating; confusion, strange behaviour or slurred speech; collapse or fits
How serious
Serious: it can turn into heatstroke if the person keeps working
A **medical emergency**: the body can no longer cool itself, and the person can die
What to do

Stop work; move to a cool, shaded place; loosen or remove heavy clothing; cool with water and fanning; give water to sip; do not let the person go back to work that day; get medical help if he or she does not improve quickly

Call **110** at once; move the person to shade; cool them as fast as you can with water, wet cloths and fanning, and cold packs at the neck, armpits and groin; give nothing to drink if they are confused or not fully awake; stay with them

blocks.note: Treat any confused or collapsed worker in the heat as heatstroke until a doctor says otherwise. Cooling quickly saves lives.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Report every **accident** (someone hurt or something damaged), every **near miss** (nothing was hurt or damaged, but it could easily have been), and every **dangerous occurrence** (such as a crane load dropping, or a fire). Near misses are free lessons: the same causes that gave a near miss today give an injury tomorrow.

ul: Record it in the incident book or on the incident form as soon as possible.
Serious accidents must also be reported to the authorities as the law and your company's procedure require; in Jamaica, that is the Ministry of Labour and Social Security.
Look at the reports together: three near misses with unchained gas cylinders in one month is a pattern. Find the cause, fix it, and brief the team.

flow: Make the scene safe and care for anyone hurt; get first aid and medical help
Preserve the scene as far as it is safe; keep others back
Collect evidence: photos, measurements, a sketch, the equipment (for example a burst disc and its markings), documents such as inspection tags, training records and the JSA
Interview the injured person and the witnesses one at a time, as soon as possible, with open questions; write down what each says in his or her own words
Work out the sequence of events, then the immediate causes and the root causes
Recommend corrective actions, using the order of controls, each with a name and a date
Write the report, present it to the manager, and follow up until every action is done

head: Level of cause
Meaning
Example: a grinding disc burst and cut a worker's arm
rows: Immediate cause
The unsafe act or condition at the moment it happened
A disc rated below the grinder's speed was fitted, and the guard had been removed
Underlying causes
Why that act or condition was there
The store held the wrong discs; the worker had not been trained to check disc ratings
Root cause
The failure in the system that allowed it
No system for buying the right discs and checking discs and guards before use

blocks.p: Ask **'why?'** again and again until you reach something the organisation can fix. A recommendation such as 'be more careful' does not fix anything; 'buy only discs rated for our grinders, add a disc and guard check to the pre-start checklist, and train all grinder users by Friday' does.

ul: Date, time and exact place; the people involved and the witnesses.
What happened, in time order, as facts, not opinions.
The injury or damage, and the first aid given.
The immediate, underlying and root causes, with the evidence for each.
Corrective actions, each with a person responsible and a date, and how they will be checked.
Signed and dated, sent to the people who need it, and kept on file.

blocks.p: A **safety inspection** is a planned walk round the workplace to find hazards before they hurt anyone. It is useful only if it uses a checklist and its findings are acted on.

flow: Plan: use a checklist made for the shop, and choose a time when work is going on
Walk the whole area with another person, such as a worker or safety representative; look and ask questions
Record each fault, where it is, and how serious it is; take photos
Deal with anything dangerous at once, for example take a damaged lead out of use
Put the findings on an action list: what, who and by when
Report to the manager and share the results with the team
Check that each action has been done, then sign it off; look for faults that keep coming back

blocks.p: A checklist for a fabrication shop usually covers: walkways and exits; housekeeping; machine guards; power leads and welding cables; gas cylinders; extraction and ventilation; fire equipment; first aid and eyewash; PPE; chemicals and their SDSs; lifting gear tags; and signs.

blocks.note: If an inspection finds the same fault week after week, fixing it each time is not enough. Ask why it keeps happening: no storage space, no one responsible, a rule that does not work in practice. Fix that.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain the safety duties of employers, supervisors and workers, and workers' rights to know, take part and refuse.
I can describe a good safety culture and supervise trainees safely.
I can tell a hazard from a risk, break a job into steps and complete a JSA.
I can score risks with a 5 × 5 matrix, say what the score means, and find the residual risk.
I can choose controls in the right order and give a welding example of each level.
I can explain the health effects of welding fume from mild, galvanised and stainless steel, and how to control them.
I can explain why chlorinated solvents and shielding gases are dangerous near welding.
I can choose and fit-check a respirator, and say why a beard spoils the seal.
I can find what I need on a safety data sheet and read hazard pictograms.
I can recognise harmful noise and heat, and control them.
I can control electric shock risks, especially in hot, damp and cramped places.
I can carry out lockout and tagout, alone and as part of a group.
I can plan hot work with a permit and a fire watch, and choose the right extinguisher.
I can store, move and use gas cylinders safely, and deal with a leak, a backfire or a flashback.
I can plan safe entry to a confined space and explain the standby person's role.
I can plan work at height in the right order and choose suitable access.
I can work out the weight of steel and plan a safe manual or crane lift, checking the lifting gear.
I can raise the alarm, evacuate, and give first aid for burns, eye injuries, shock, cuts and heat illness.
I can report and investigate an incident, find its root cause and write the report.
I can carry out a safety inspection and follow actions through until they are closed.

terms: An enclosed space with limited ways in and out, where bad air can build up
The written approval needed before anyone enters a confined space
Removing a hazard completely: the highest level of control
A trained person posted to look out for fires during and after hot work
A flame burning back inside the torch or hose
A device at the regulator or torch that stops a flashback reaching the hose and cylinder
Heat illness with heavy sweating, dizziness and sickness; the person is still thinking clearly
The most serious heat illness: the body can no longer cool itself, and the person may become confused
Written permission, with precautions, for welding, cutting or grinding outside the welding shop
Job safety analysis: a form that lists each step of a job, its hazards and controls
Local exhaust ventilation: extraction that captures fume at the source
Locking and tagging an isolator so a machine cannot be started during work
Flu-like illness from breathing zinc or other metal fume
An event that could have caused harm but did not
A very toxic gas that forms when arc light acts on chlorinated solvent vapour
The risk left after all the controls are in place
The likelihood that a hazard causes harm, combined with how bad the harm would be
The underlying failure in the system that must be fixed to stop an incident happening again
The most a piece of lifting equipment may lift
Safety data sheet: the supplier's 16-section sheet on a product's hazards and safe use
How bad the harm would be; multiplied by likelihood to give the risk score
Replacing a hazard with something less hazardous
A device that lowers a welding machine's open-circuit voltage when not welding

c1.title: A juice tank in Bog Walk
c1.text: Sheldon leads a team asked to weld a new outlet flange inside a 2.5 m diameter stainless-steel tank at a food factory in Bog Walk, St Catherine. The only way in is a 600 mm manway on top. The tank held orange juice and was washed out yesterday with a cleaning chemical. The weld will be made by TIG, with argon shielding gas. The factory's engineer is preparing the confined space entry permit, and Sheldon has a gas detector. It is 31 °C outside.

c2.title: Roof truss repairs at a church hall in Christiana
c2.text: Latoya's team will weld new steel plates to the exposed roof trusses of a church hall in Christiana, Manchester, about 5 m above the floor. Timber boards are fixed above the trusses, under the roof sheets. Below are wooden pews, and curtains hang on the stage. The team owns ladders and can hire a mobile elevating work platform (MEWP) with trained operators. Latoya's risk matrix scores likelihood and severity from 1 to 5 and multiplies them; her workplace treats 12 to 16 as high.

c3.title: A school fence in Lucea
c3.text: Damion's team is to fix 60 galvanised posts and mesh panels for a new fence at a primary school in Lucea, Hanover, during term time. The plan is to weld the panels to the posts on site, using an engine-driven welder. One welder, Courtney, has a full beard and has been given a disposable respirator rated for welding fume. Last month another welder had chills, fever and aches on the evening after welding galvanised steel.

c4.title: Inside a shipping container in Kingston
c4.text: Winsome supervises two welders converting a steel shipping container into a site office at a yard in Kingston. It is July, about 33 °C in the shade and much hotter inside the container. The welders grind window openings and weld frames inside, with one door open. They have to shout to be heard at arm's length. By 2 p.m. one welder, Tyrone, has a headache, feels dizzy and sick, and is sweating heavily; his skin is pale and clammy, but he is thinking clearly.

c5.title: Near misses at a steel yard in Portmore
c5.text: Mr Bryan manages a steel yard in Portmore, St Catherine. This month a sheet of 10 mm plate, 2.4 m × 1.2 m, swung and hit a rack while being lifted on a single chain sling. A worker removed a 'Do not operate' tag from the isolator of the guillotine, which had no lock on it, to finish a cut while the fitter repairing it was at lunch. And for the third week running, the weekly inspection found the side fire exit blocked by bundles of steel.

questions.q: Why is the argon shielding gas a particular danger inside this tank?
o: It is heavier than air and can push out the oxygen
It is poisonous to breathe, even in small amounts
It catches fire easily if it meets a spark from the arc
It reacts with stainless steel to make a toxic fume
questions.why: Argon is not poisonous and does not burn, but it is heavier than air. In a tank it builds up from the bottom and displaces oxygen, and a welder can collapse without warning; that is why the air is tested and the tank ventilated.

questions.q: Before entry, the gas detector at the manway reads 19.0% oxygen. What should Sheldon do?
o: Let the welder go in, since 19% is close enough to normal air
Blow oxygen into the tank to bring the level back up
Let the welder go in wearing a disposable dust mask
Keep everyone out, ventilate with fresh air, and test again
questions.why: Normal air has about 20.9% oxygen, and most permits forbid entry below about 19.5%. Fresh air is blown in and the air re-tested at several levels; oxygen is never used, as it makes clothing burn fiercely, and a dust mask does not supply oxygen.

questions.q: What is the standby person's main job while the welder is inside the tank?
o: Go in to help straight away if the welder seems unwell
Fetch tools and materials from the store when they are needed
Stay at the manway, keep in contact, and raise the alarm
Watch the welding closely to check the quality of the weld
questions.why: Many people who die in confined spaces are untrained rescuers who went in after a colleague. The standby person stays at the entry, keeps in contact, never goes in, and starts the rescue plan.

questions.q: Why must Sheldon find out exactly which chemical was used to wash out the tank?
o: It decides which filler rod the TIG welder must use on the flange
Its residue may give off harmful gas, so the controls must allow for it
It changes the colour of the finished weld, which the client may reject
It sets how long the tank must stand full of water before welding
questions.why: Cleaning chemicals can leave residues that give off harmful vapour or gas, especially when heated by welding. The SDS tells Sheldon what to test for and which controls and PPE are needed before entry.

questions.q: Why is welding from a ladder particularly dangerous?
o: Sparks can weaken a ladder's rungs within a few minutes
A ladder stops the welding extraction from working properly
A shock, a flash or a burn can make the welder fall
Ladders may be used only outdoors, never inside a hall
questions.why: A welder on a ladder has little to hold and cannot react safely to a tingle of shock, a flash or a hot drop of spatter. Use a platform with guardrails, such as the MEWP, so a startled reaction does not become a fall.

questions.q: What should the hot work plan include for the pews and stage curtains below?
o: Weld quickly in short runs so that fewer sparks fall
Move or cover them, and post a fire watch at floor level
Ask the pastor to keep all the hall doors shut during the work
Keep an extinguisher in the van parked outside the hall
questions.why: Sparks and spatter fall a long way and can smoulder in fabric and timber. Move what can be moved, cover the rest with fire-resisting blankets, and keep a fire watch where the sparks land, during and after the work.

questions.q: If the team works from a MEWP basket wearing harnesses, why must their lanyards be suitable for hot work?
o: Ordinary webbing can melt or burn through from sparks and spatter
Hot-work lanyards are shorter, so the welder cannot reach the trusses
Ordinary lanyards conduct welding current through the harness
The law allows only steel lanyards inside a church building
questions.why: Synthetic webbing can be weakened or cut by spatter without anyone noticing. Lanyards made for hot work, for example with a steel wire core, keep their strength when sparks land on them.

questions.q: Latoya scores a fire in the timber boards above the trusses as possible (3) × major (4). What does this mean?
o: 6: low, so the work can go ahead with normal care
7: medium, so it can go ahead if it is supervised
12: high, so add controls before work starts
20: very high, so the job can never go ahead at all
questions.why: 3 × 4 = 12, which her workplace treats as high: work must not start until further controls, such as fire-resisting shields between the weld and the boards and a fire watch, bring it down.

questions.q: Which option is highest in the order of controls for the zinc fume?
o: Grind the zinc off and weld with the wind at the welder's back
Give every welder a respirator rated for welding fume
Limit each welder to two hours of welding a day
Fix the panels with bolted clamps, so no welding is needed
questions.why: Bolting removes the hot work, and with it the zinc fume: elimination is the highest control. Grinding and wind direction reduce the fume, time limits are administrative, and respirators are PPE, the last line of defence.

questions.q: Why is Courtney's disposable respirator unlikely to protect him?
o: Disposable masks cannot stop zinc fume at all
His beard stops it sealing, so fume leaks in at the edges
It will melt from the heat given off by the arc
It is made only for oxy-fuel work, not for electric arc welding
questions.why: A tight-fitting respirator works only if it seals to the skin; through a beard, fume takes the easy path round the edges. A loose-fitting powered respirator, such as a helmet with filtered air, protects a bearded welder.

questions.q: How should the engine-driven welder be refuelled?
o: With the engine off and cooled, away from the welding and sparks
With the engine running, so that the welding does not have to stop
Inside the school's store room, out of the sun and the rain
Beside the weld, so that the leads can reach the work more easily
questions.why: Fuel vapour can be lit by a hot engine, a spark or the arc. Stop the engine, let it cool, refuel away from hot work, and store the fuel can safely; keep the machine outdoors, where its exhaust cannot build up.

questions.q: What do Tyrone's signs point to, and what should Winsome do?
o: Heatstroke: give him ice water and let him carry on welding
Metal fume fever: send him home on the bus to sleep it off
Heat exhaustion: rest him in the shade, cool him, give water
Mild thirst: give him a soft drink and let him get back to work
questions.why: Heavy sweating, pale clammy skin, headache, dizziness and sickness, with a clear mind, are signs of heat exhaustion. He stops work, cools down and sips water, and does not return that day; if he becomes confused, it is heatstroke: call 110.

questions.q: Which change to tomorrow's plan will do most to reduce the heat risk?
o: Let the welders wear vests so that they stay a little cooler
Work straight through lunch so they finish before the worst heat
Give each welder an energy drink at midday to keep going
Work inside early, with fresh air blown in and set breaks
questions.why: Moving the heaviest work to the coolest hours, ventilating the container and planning rest breaks with water all reduce heat stress. Vests expose skin to arc burns, and skipping breaks makes heat illness more likely.

questions.q: Why is the grinding noise worse inside the container than in the open yard?
o: The steel walls reflect the sound, so it builds up inside
Hot air makes sound travel louder than cool air does
A grinder runs faster when it is used in a closed-in space
Steel makes grinding discs vibrate at a higher speed
questions.why: Sound bounces off hard steel walls instead of spreading out, so the same tool is louder inside. Having to shout at arm's length means the level is harmful: hearing protection must be worn all the time they are in there.

questions.q: Which is the best way to control the welding fume inside the container?
o: Open the one door wider and rely on the breeze to clear the fume
Weld only after 4 p.m., when the container is cooler
Extraction at the weld, vented outside, plus a fresh-air fan
Give each welder a cotton cloth to tie over the nose
questions.why: Local exhaust ventilation captures fume at the source and takes it outside, and a fan blowing in fresh air stops it building up in the enclosed space. A cloth gives no real protection against fine fume.

questions.q: About how much does the 10 mm plate weigh? (Steel weighs about 7,850 kg per cubic metre.)
o: About 226 kg
About 113 kg
About 23 kg
About 2,260 kg
questions.why: Volume = 2.4 m × 1.2 m × 0.010 m = 0.0288 m³; weight = 0.0288 × 7,850 ≈ 226 kg. Knowing the weight is the first step in choosing lifting gear with enough safe working load.

questions.q: What should change for the next lift of this plate?
o: Lift it faster, so that it has less time to swing
Use horizontal plate clamps on a two-leg sling, with a tag line
Have a worker steady it by hand from underneath the load
Keep the single sling, but lift the plate higher off the ground
questions.why: A single sling lets a flat plate tilt, swing and slide out. Paired plate clamps on a two-leg sling hold it level, and a tag line controls swing from a safe distance; nobody goes under a suspended load.

questions.q: How should Mr Bryan treat the removal of the guillotine's tag?
o: As minor, since the fitter was away at lunch at the time
By removing all tags at lunchtime to avoid any confusion
By letting the worker finish, and mentioning it to him later
As a serious near miss: investigate, and add locks to tags
questions.why: If the fitter had come back and reached into the blade, the cut could have been fatal. Only the person who fitted a lock or tag may remove it; a tag alone is only a warning, so the isolator should also have been locked off.

questions.q: The side exit has been blocked three weeks running. Which question will best find the root cause?
o: Which worker left the bundles of steel there this week?
Why does the steel end up there: is there nowhere else?
How many times has the exit been blocked so far this year?
Is the exit sign above the side door still lit properly?
questions.why: Clearing the exit each week deals only with the symptom. Asking why the steel keeps going there (no storage space, deliveries put down in the nearest gap, no one responsible) finds what must change so the exit stays clear.

questions.q: While cutting, a welder hears a squealing hiss in the oxy-acetylene torch and the handle gets hot. What should be done first?
o: Turn the oxygen up to blow the flame back out of the torch
Drop the torch and run from the area as fast as possible
Close the torch valves at once, then the cylinder valves
Bend the hoses over by hand to cut off the gas flow
questions.why: These are signs of a flashback: the flame is burning inside the torch. Close the torch valves at once (most makers say oxygen first), then the cylinder valves, and do not use the equipment again until the cause is found and it has been checked.
